ranking.rationale: BMI is one of the strongest and most causally stable predictors of diabetes risk in BRFSS, with a direct physiological relationship that should generalize across states and years better than healthcare-access, demographic, or domain-identifier features. The continuous version preserves more signal than the coarser BMI category encodings.

High blood pressure is a strong, clinically meaningful comorbidity/risk marker for diabetes that should remain predictive across domains. It adds substantial stable signal beyond BMI, unlike redundant BMI category encodings or brittle domain/healthcare-access proxies such as state, year, checkup, or insurance.

Physical inactivity is a well-established, semantically stable diabetes risk factor that adds complementary lifestyle information beyond BMI and hypertension, while being less likely than state, year, healthcare-access, or socioeconomic variables to encode domain-specific shortcuts.

High cholesterol is a clinically meaningful cardiometabolic comorbidity that remains predictive of diabetes risk across domains. It adds stable health-status signal beyond BMI, hypertension, and physical activity, while being less domain-identifying or shortcut-prone than state, year, insurance, income, education, or healthcare-utilization features. Avoid redundant encodings of already selected variables.

History of stroke is a strong, semantically stable cardiometabolic comorbidity signal for diabetes risk and adds complementary health-status information beyond BMI, hypertension, cholesterol, and physical activity, while avoiding obvious domain-ID features like state/year and weaker demographic shortcuts.

Adds a strong, semantically stable cardiometabolic comorbidity signal beyond BMI, hypertension, cholesterol, inactivity, and stroke. Coronary heart disease/MI is closely linked to long-run diabetes risk and complications, while being less likely than state, year, healthcare-access, or socioeconomic variables to act as a domain identifier or brittle shortcut.

Sex adds strong, biologically grounded diabetes risk signal that should remain stable across domains, while being less likely than state, year, healthcare-access, or socioeconomic variables to act as a domain identifier or brittle shortcut. It is also complementary to the already selected cardiometabolic and activity features.

Adds a strong, semantically stable cardiometabolic comorbidity signal beyond BMI, hypertension, cholesterol, stroke, activity, and sex. Prior heart disease history is robustly associated with diabetes risk across domains and is less likely than state, year, healthcare-access, or socioeconomic variables to act mainly as a domain shortcut.

Complements the already selected hypertension indicator with the opposite category, letting the model represent this strong, medically stable diabetes risk factor cleanly. It adds more robust signal than socioeconomic, access-to-care, year, or state features, which are more domain-dependent or shortcut-prone.

Physical-health burden is a strong, semantically stable correlate of diabetes and adds complementary signal beyond BMI, hypertension, cholesterol, cardiovascular history, activity, and sex. It is less likely than state, year, healthcare-access, or socioeconomic variables to act mainly as a domain identifier or shortcut.

Adds a strong, clinically relevant metabolic comorbidity signal beyond BMI, hypertension, activity, and cardiovascular history. High cholesterol is semantically tied to diabetes risk and should transfer across domains better than state, year, healthcare-access, or socioeconomic shortcut features; this category complements the already selected positive indicator for TOLDHI.

Adds the complementary TOTINDA indicator level to the already selected exercise feature, capturing a robust lifestyle risk factor for diabetes that should generalize across domains better than state, year, healthcare-access, or socioeconomic shortcut variables.

Alcohol consumption adds a new, behaviorally causal risk factor for diabetes that is likely to remain predictive across domains. It complements already selected obesity, hypertension, cholesterol, cardiovascular history, sex, physical activity, and general health features with relatively low redundancy, while avoiding brittle domain identifiers like state/year and weaker socioeconomic or healthcare-access proxies.

Mental-health burden adds nonredundant health-status signal beyond BMI, hypertension, cholesterol, activity, CVD, sex, and drinking. It is plausibly linked to diabetes risk and self-management through stress, depression, and overall morbidity, while being less of a direct domain identifier or socioeconomic shortcut than state, year, income, education, insurance, or care-access variables.

Adds access-to-care signal that is plausibly and stably related to diabetes burden and management, while being less redundant with already selected cardiometabolic and lifestyle features than BMI/cholesterol duplicates. It is more semantically predictive across domains than state/year identifiers and less shortcut-prone than income or education.

Recent cholesterol screening adds stable clinical-risk information complementary to BMI, hypertension, cholesterol diagnosis, activity, and cardiovascular history. It is more semantically tied to diabetes risk/management than state/year or socioeconomic proxies, while avoiding redundant duplicate encodings already partly covered by selected features.

Adds a broadly stable access-to-care signal not yet covered by the selected set. In BRFSS diabetes prediction, inability to afford needed care is associated with worse chronic disease burden and under-managed risk, and is less domain-identifying than state/year features. It complements BMI, hypertension, cholesterol, activity, and general health without relying on brittle geographic or socioeconomic shortcuts as strongly as state, income, or education.

Health coverage adds stable signal about access to diagnosis and treatment, which is relevant for self-reported diabetes beyond already selected cardiometabolic and activity features. It is less domain-identifying and less brittle than state/year, and offers more marginal value than redundant category expansions or missingness indicators.

Recent routine checkup adds stable signal about healthcare engagement and diagnosis opportunity for diabetes beyond BMI, hypertension, cholesterol, activity, and coverage, while being less domain-specific than state/year and less shortcut-prone than SES or marital variables.

Education adds stable, non-domain-specific signal about diabetes risk via health literacy, socioeconomic conditions, and long-run behavior. It is less brittle than state/year identifiers and less redundant than additional encodings of already selected variables.

Income adds strong marginal signal for diabetes risk through stable socioeconomic pathways affecting diet, access, stress, and chronic disease burden. It is less domain-identifying than state/year features and less redundant than additional encodings of already selected variables.

Vegetable consumption adds a plausible, semantically stable lifestyle risk signal for diabetes that is not yet covered by the selected set. It is less domain-identifying than state/year features and less redundant than additional one-hot bins for already selected variables like BMI, income, checkup, or cholesterol.

Smoking history adds a well-established, semantically stable cardiometabolic risk factor not yet covered by the selected set. It should generalize better across domains than state/year or missingness indicators, and is less redundant than additional one-hot levels of already selected variables.

Fruit intake adds a plausible, domain-stable lifestyle signal for diabetes risk that is not yet covered by the selected set. It is less likely than state, year, missingness, or extra healthcare-access encodings to act as a domain identifier, and offers more new information than redundant category splits of already selected variables.

Adds a broadly causal lifestyle signal—low vegetable intake is a stable diabetes risk correlate across domains—and complements already selected BMI, activity, fruit, smoking, alcohol, and cardiometabolic history features with less shortcut risk than state, year, missingness, or redundant duplicate encodings.

Adds smoking-history information beyond current/ever-smoking proxies already chosen. Lifetime smoking is a broadly stable cardiometabolic risk factor linked to diabetes and should transfer across domains better than state/year identifiers or missingness artifacts, while offering cleaner marginal value than redundant category expansions of already selected variables.

Adds a robust nonlinear obesity threshold signal beyond continuous BMI, which is strongly and semantically linked to diabetes risk across domains; more stable and less domain-identifying than state/year or missingness indicators, and less redundant than additional healthcare-access or duplicate category dummies.

Adds the complementary stroke-history indicator to the already selected no-stroke category, capturing a clinically stable diabetes comorbidity signal with high marginal value while avoiding brittle domain identifiers like state or year.

Adds the obese/overweight BMI category signal in a thresholded form that is highly and stably related to diabetes risk across domains. It complements continuous BMI5 by capturing nonlinear risk without relying on brittle geography, year, or demographic shortcut features, and is more semantically robust than remaining access/missingness/state indicators.

Adds the remaining BMI-category signal beyond continuous BMI and existing normal/overweight indicators: underweight is rare and less relevant, while the obese category is largely captured by high BMI. This category can capture nonlinear diabetes risk in a semantically stable way across domains, unlike state/year or missingness indicators.

Completes the BMI category signal with the obese category, a strong and semantically stable diabetes risk factor across domains; it adds useful nonlinear risk information beyond continuous BMI and the already selected lower BMI-category indicators, while avoiding domain-ID or leakage features.

Adds complementary stable signal about preventive care and cardiometabolic risk beyond the already selected cholesterol-check category, while avoiding brittle domain identifiers like state/year and weaker shortcut-heavy demographics.

Adds the missing complementary fruit-intake category, a plausible lifestyle risk factor for diabetes that should transfer across domains better than state/year or missingness indicators, and it is less redundant than additional checkup/cholesterol/SES one-hot levels already partly covered.

Adds the missing complementary level of health coverage, a stable access-to-care signal linked to diabetes diagnosis/management, with low risk of domain leakage compared with state/year or missingness indicators and less redundancy than more one-hot levels of already-covered variables.

Current smoking status adds stable cardiometabolic risk information beyond lifetime smoking, BMI, activity, diet, hypertension, and cholesterol. It is more semantically predictive across domains than state/year or missingness indicators, and likely offers better marginal value than additional healthcare-utilization or socioeconomic category dummies already partly covered.

Adds stable incremental signal by distinguishing current smoking status among ever-smokers, which is more semantically relevant to diabetes risk than more missingness or domain-coded features. It complements already selected SMOKE100 and lifestyle variables without relying on brittle state/year identifiers or leakage-prone artifacts.

Binge drinking adds a distinct, behavior-based diabetes risk signal beyond total alcohol volume, smoking, BMI, activity, and diet. It is semantically stable across domains and less likely than state/year or missingness indicators to encode domain identity or survey artifacts.

Adds complementary alcohol-risk signal beyond drinks-per-week and current binge-drinking category is more semantically tied to diabetes risk than demographic or domain-coded candidates. It is likely to generalize across domains and is preferable to state/year/missingness features or redundant one-hot expansions already partly covered.

Adds complementary socioeconomic signal beyond the already selected income-low and education-college indicators. A lower-income bracket is a stable correlate of diabetes risk through access, diet, stress, and care patterns, while being less domain-identifying than state/year and less brittle than missingness or not-asked indicators.

Adds low-education signal not yet covered by the single college-graduate indicator already selected. Education is a stable socioeconomic risk factor for diabetes through health literacy, diet, and access patterns, and is less domain-identifying than state/year features and less brittle than missingness or not-asked indicators.

Adds remaining education signal with likely stable cross-domain relevance for diabetes risk via health literacy and socioeconomic status. It complements already selected EDUCA_10 and EDUCA_50 without introducing obvious domain-ID leakage, and is preferable to state/year or missingness indicators and to more redundant healthcare-utilization categories.

Adds remaining education signal beyond already selected lower/mid categories; college-graduate status is a stable socioeconomic predictor of diabetes risk and self-management, with less domain-specific leakage than state/year or missingness indicators.

Adds the remaining meaningful education level contrast (some high school) to an already partially selected socioeconomic gradient. Education is a stable, semantically relevant correlate of diabetes risk through health literacy, occupation, and lifestyle, and is less domain-identifying than state/year features and less brittle than missingness indicators.

Adds the remaining informative education level (college graduate) from an already selected stable socioeconomic variable. This can improve calibration beyond the existing EDUCA categories while remaining more semantically robust across domains than state, year, missingness, or healthcare-access artifacts.

Adds the missing major non-missing checkup category from an already useful healthcare-utilization signal. Recent routine checkup is a broadly stable proxy for preventive care and diagnosis opportunity across domains, with less domain-leakage risk than state/year and more marginal value than missingness or additional socioeconomic one-hots already partly covered.

Marital status adds stable health-behavior and social-support signal that can improve diabetes risk prediction beyond BMI, cardiometabolic history, smoking, income, and education, while being less domain-identifying and less brittle than state/year or missingness indicators.

Adds marital-status signal beyond the already selected married indicator, capturing stable social-support and household-pattern differences associated with diabetes risk, while avoiding obvious domain-ID features like state/year and offering more marginal value than additional missingness or redundant utilization-category indicators.

Adds a new low-income category beyond the already selected income bins, capturing a robust socioeconomic gradient in diabetes risk that should generalize across domains better than state/year identifiers or missingness/refusal indicators, and offers more marginal value than additional checkup/marital/missing-category features.

Adds the remaining substantive routine-checkup category beyond already selected recent-checkup indicators; healthcare utilization is a stable diabetes correlate, while avoiding brittle state/year/domain-ID features and low-value missingness/refusal indicators.

Adds a new nonredundant income stratum beyond the already selected low-income bins, capturing a stable socioeconomic gradient in diabetes risk without relying on explicit domain identifiers like state/year or brittle missingness indicators.

It is more semantically predictive and less domain-identifying than year/state or missing/refusal features, and likely offers better marginal value than additional socioeconomic or marital one-hot categories already partly covered.

Adds remaining socioeconomic signal as a mid-income category after lower-income bins are already selected; income is a stable, semantically relevant diabetes risk correlate, while this is less brittle than state/year or missingness indicators and more useful than additional refusal/not-asked categories.

It is more robust across domains than state, year, or missingness indicators, and offers cleaner marginal value than additional socioeconomic or utilization-category dummies already partly covered.

Income is a stable upstream correlate of diabetes risk and care access across domains, while this category is less brittle than state/year identifiers and more informative than missing/refusal indicators or redundant not-asked codes.

Adds useful stable signal about access to care/insurance gaps beyond existing health coverage indicators, especially for the ineligible-or-missing group, while avoiding brittle state features and low-value missing/refusal artifacts.

Adds a remaining non-missing marital-status category with some stable incremental signal through household/social support and age-life-course structure, while avoiding brittle state/domain identifiers and low-value missingness/refusal indicators.

Income is a broadly stable correlate of diabetes risk via diet, healthcare access, and chronic stress, and is less domain-identifying than state or missingness indicators. It should add more marginal signal than additional checkup/marital categories or refusal/missing artifacts.

This should improve coverage of the monotonic SES gradient without relying on brittle domain identifiers like state or missingness/refusal indicators.

High cholesterol is a stable diabetes comorbidity/risk marker across domains, and this category is preferable to state, year-adjacent missingness, or other refusal/missing indicators that are more likely to encode survey artifacts than robust disease risk.

Adds a remaining non-missing marital-status category with plausible stable signal through household/social support and life-course structure, while avoiding strong domain-ID leakage from STATE and avoiding brittle missing/refusal indicators. Adds the remaining informative cholesterol-status category (refused/unknown) after yes/no are already included. Cholesterol history is a stable diabetes risk correlate across domains, and this offers more marginal signal than additional checkup/income/marital categories while avoiding highly domain-identifying STATE features and brittle missingness indicators.

Adds remaining non-missing income information likely still useful after lower/mid income bins are selected; socioeconomic status is a stable diabetes correlate, while this high-income category can improve calibration with less OOD risk than state or missing/refusal indicators.

Adds the remaining substantive CHECKUP1 category (5+ years since routine checkup), which can stably capture low preventive care engagement and underdiagnosis risk beyond already selected recent-checkup categories. It is more semantically meaningful and OOD-robust than state or missing/refusal indicators, and less redundant than additional socioeconomic or missingness dummies.

Adds the remaining nonresponse/unknown income category, completing a strong and generally stable socioeconomic risk signal already shown useful by the selected income bins. This is more semantically relevant to diabetes risk than missing-value indicators for other variables, and avoids brittle domain-ID features like state or not-asked patterns.

Adds current smoking-status missingness/not-asked information, which can still carry health-behavior signal beyond SMOKE100 and existing SMOKDAY2 categories, while avoiding brittle state/domain identifiers and offering more marginal value than other remaining options that are mostly refusal/missing flags or demographic artifacts.

Adds a still-unused substantive marital-status category rather than a missingness or state/domain indicator. Marital status can capture stable household/social-support structure linked to diabetes risk and management, while being less brittle than STATE and less redundant than additional missing-value flags.

Adds the remaining meaningful CHECKUP1 category ('never') after other checkup recency bins are already included. This can capture durable lack of preventive care/access behavior linked to undiagnosed or unmanaged diabetes risk, while avoiding brittle state/domain identifiers and being more semantically useful than missing/refused indicators.

Education is a broadly stable social determinant of diabetes risk and self-management that should transfer across BRFSS domains. The non-missing education levels are already included, so adding the missing/refused indicator can recover useful signal from nonresponse patterns without introducing the strong domain-ID leakage risk of state features or the low-value redundancy of many other remaining missing-category dummies.

Adds a clinically relevant, broadly stable screening signal for cardiometabolic risk that is not yet covered by the selected set; among remaining options it offers more semantic predictive value than missing/refusal indicators and avoids brittle domain-ID features like state.

History of stroke is a strong, semantically stable comorbidity signal for diabetes risk and complications. The informative yes/no stroke indicators are already selected, so the remaining marginal value comes from capturing unresolved/refused stroke responses, which can preserve signal without introducing the severe domain-leakage risk of state features or the low-value redundancy of other missing-category indicators.

High blood pressure is a strong, semantically stable diabetes correlate, and the missing/unknown indicator can add marginal signal beyond the yes/no dummies already selected by capturing nonresponse patterns tied to health status and care access. It is still preferable to state features, which are domain identifiers, and likely more useful than other remaining missing-category indicators.

Adds the remaining physical-activity missing/unknown indicator, complementing already selected activity categories. Physical inactivity is a robust diabetes risk factor across domains, and this feature can recover signal from respondents not covered by existing TOTINDA dummies without relying on brittle state/domain identifiers or stronger shortcut features.

Adds a plausible, semantically stable lifestyle risk signal not yet covered; vegetable intake complements BMI, activity, fruit, smoking, alcohol, and cardiometabolic history, while avoiding brittle domain-ID features like STATE and low-value missingness indicators.

Fruit intake is a plausible, semantically stable lifestyle correlate of diabetes risk and adds nonredundant health-behavior signal beyond BMI, activity, smoking, alcohol, and vegetable intake. State features are strong domain identifiers and should be avoided for OOD generalization; the remaining candidates are mostly missingness/refusal indicators with lower stable predictive value.

Most other remaining options are either explicit domain identifiers (STATE), likely brittle missingness/artifact indicators, or low-value refusal categories already largely covered by selected socioeconomic and healthcare-use features.

Binge drinking status adds a plausible, behavior-based diabetes risk signal that should transfer across domains better than state or year identifiers. It is less redundant than remaining smoking/checkup missingness indicators and avoids brittle geographic shortcut features.

Current smoking status adds plausible diabetes-related behavioral signal beyond lifetime smoking history, while remaining more semantically stable across domains than state indicators or missing/refusal categories.
